messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The summer Amira’s twenty-three-year-old son, Tariq, collapsed from septic shock, the world narrowed to the sterile, antiseptic air of the intensive care unit and the relentless rhythm of dialysis pumps. She watched nurses adjust IV drips and overheard physicians quietly discuss prognosis with families already preparing for loss. That night became the anchor of her trauma. When the sharp, chemical scent of a hospital corridor or the glint of a syringe surfaced in her daily life, it did not merely recall the past; the uncontrolled access of her trauma memory would seize her, dumping the full, unfiltered emotional intensity of that ICU night without any clear image. The visceral force of these sudden surges immediately convinced her that she had permanently altered for the worse, that her professional identity as a compassionate social worker had been stripped away by profound helplessness. That conviction, paired with the belief that she simply could not stop bad things from happening to those she cared about, dictated her daily choices. She stopped going out to neighborhood gatherings, strictly avoided medical cues like ambulance sirens and physical examinations, and relied on thought suppression, forcing herself to push the recollections out of her mind during work hours. As the following months unfolded, this pattern calcified into a quiet but inescapable feedback loop. Her conviction of permanent damage and helplessness acted as a cognitive lens that warped how her memories surfaced. Instead of fading with time, the recollections were systematically amplified by her belief that the trauma had permanently altered her, making the sudden, imageless emotional surges feel even more invasive and inescapable. Simultaneously, those negative appraisals sharpened her attention to loss themes. She found herself scanning every group discussion or client intake for whispers about bereavement, her heightened vigilance ensuring that ordinary conversations about grief suddenly felt dangerously amplified. When she fixated on those loss themes, they did not remain abstract; they triggered the next wave of uncontrolled, imageless recall, leaving her breathless and disoriented in the middle of a home visit. The cycle tightened further when her avoidance strategies quietly confirmed her worst fears. By retreating from medical settings and suppressing her thoughts, she systematically eliminated the very opportunities to disprove her helplessness, leaving the belief that she was fundamentally changed for the worse to remain unchallenged and absolute. She continued to work as a social worker, but her daily environment became a carefully controlled space. She relocated her caseload to a quiet community outreach office, deliberately routing her walks away from clinic entrances, and she still flinched when a visiting nurse approached a senior client with a vein finder and needles. During routine wellness checks, the mere sight of medical equipment would trigger a spike of panic, forcing her to excuse herself and retreat to her car. These clinical encounters reinforced her core beliefs: every time she witnessed a patient’s deterioration, her negative appraisals flared, convincing her that her own helplessness was contagious and that she had permanently damaged her capacity to protect anyone. To survive the emotional weight, she relied on thought suppression, mentally rehearsing case notes to drown out the grief on recall. Yet this very suppression only deepened her conviction that she was fundamentally changed for the worse, because avoiding the feelings prevented her from processing them, ensuring that the negative appraisals remained intact. Now at eighty, Amira seeks therapy not because the symptoms have intensified, but because the exhaustion of maintaining this quiet vigilance is fracturing her remaining relationships and her professional identity. She is most afraid that her avoidance has quietly isolated her from the community she spent a lifetime serving, and what she hopes for is simply to reclaim the ability to move through her days without bracing for another collapse that never comes.
